processing: Made as raw pu-erh usually is: wilted, pan-fired, rolled and sun-dried, then pressed or kept loose. The same leaf is also sold in other styles.
harvest_season: Spring is the usual prized picking, as across Lincang.
appearance_dry: Large dark strips, in keeping with the generally dark leaf of Yongde teas.
appearance_wet: Thick large leaves in yellow-green to olive.
taste_profile: Full, brisk and thick yet smooth, with a quiet fragrance; young tea is noted for marked bitterness and astringency that soften after some storage into a fast returning sweetness.

brewing.notes: Young Mangfei can be hard going: use slightly cooler water and very short first steeps, or give it some storage.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, as cakes or loose mao cha. Tasters often suggest resting a young one for a while, since the bitterness eases with time. Beyond that it follows other Lincang raw teas, with tree age the main price divider; it stays relatively little known.
description:
Mangfei is a village in Mengban township, Yongde County, close to the Burmese border, and the name of the large-leaf tea grown there. Yongde gets far less attention than Mengku next door, and that keeps this one a connoisseur's tea.

The leaf belongs to the Mengban Mangfei large-leaf group, which has been recognised as a provincial improved variety. It is made into raw pu-erh in the usual way, and the leaf tends to come out dark, as Yongde teas generally do.

Expect a strong cup. Young Mangfei is known for heavy bitterness and astringency with a thick, brisk body behind it, and after some storage it is said to turn sweeter and easier. Cooler water and flash steeps help if you drink it new.

The tea has a following among Taiwanese pu-erh drinkers. Altitude figures for the garden disagree, from about 1,380 to 1,500 metres, so do not take a number on a wrapper too seriously. Ask about the tree age and the year instead.
history: Mangfei tea takes its name from the village. Around 800 villagers, about half the population, depend mainly on farming, including tea. Wider recognition in the pu-erh market is still limited.
